classification_signals: The paper reviews existing medical and biological research on light's non-visual effects (Sections 1, 2).
It frequently cites numerous external studies (e.g., Berson et al., 2002; Zeitzer et al., 2000; Küller and Wetterberg, 1993).
Figures and tables presented (e.g., Fig. 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, Table 2) explicitly attribute their data/source to other published works, not new data from this paper.
Sections 3, 4, and 5 discuss the 'practical meaning' and 'health-related quality aspects' based on the synthesized literature, proposing new lighting scenarios and standards.
title: Non-visual biological effect of lighting and the practical meaning for lighting for work

findings.antecedent: light entering human eyes
findings.consequent: non-visual biological effect on human body
findings.quote: Recent medical and biological research has consistently shown that light entering the human eyes has, apart from a visual effect, also an important non-visual biological effect on the human body.

findings.antecedent: good lighting
findings.consequent: positive influence on health, well-being, alertness, and sleep quality
findings.quote: As a consequence, good lighting has a positive influence on health, well-being, alertness, and even on sleep quality.

findings.antecedent: novel photoreceptor cell (ipRGC) in retina
findings.consequent: regulation of non-visual biological effects (circadian timing, body temperature, heart rate, cortisol production, melatonin production, alertness)
findings.quote: This novel photoreceptor cell type, an intrinsic photosensitive retinal ganglion cell (ipRGC), regulates many non-visual biological effects such as circadian timing, body temperature, heart rate, cortisol production, melatonin production and alertness

findings.antecedent: wavelength of light
findings.consequent: biological sensitivity (maximum in blue region)
findings.quote: Where the maximum visual sensitivity lies in the yellow-green wavelength region, the maximum biological sensitivity lies in the blue region of the spectrum.

findings.antecedent: light-dark rhythms (e.g., 24h rhythm of daylight)
findings.consequent: control of biological clock and regulation of important hormones
findings.quote: The most important processes are related to the control of the biological clock and to the regulation of some important hormones through regular light-dark rhythms

findings.antecedent: disruption of light-dark rhythm
findings.consequent: disruption of body rhythms (e.g., cortisol, melatonin)
findings.quote: For good health, it is important that these rhythms are not disrupted too much.

findings.antecedent: bright light in the morning
findings.consequent: restoration of normal body rhythm
findings.quote: In the event of a disruption of the rhythm, bright light in the morning helps restore the normal rhythm.

findings.antecedent: higher lighting level (1700 lux vs 450 lux) in office environment
findings.consequent: fewer delta waves in EEG (indicator of sleepiness)
findings.quote: the higher lighting level results in fewer delta waves (the delta activity of an EEG being an indicator of sleepiness), indicating that bright light has an alerting influence on the central nervous system

findings.antecedent: high-light regime (2800 lux vs 250 lux) for night-workers
findings.consequent: significantly increased arousal level, better alertness and mood
findings.quote: the high-light regime always results in a significantly increased arousal level and thus better alertness and mood.

findings.antecedent: combination of artificial light and daylight (in May, when daylight contributes substantially)
findings.consequent: lower stress complaint level
findings.quote: But in May, when daylight really contributes, the group benefiting from daylight has a considerably lower stress complaint level.

findings.antecedent: vertical illuminance at eye level at daytime working place
findings.consequent: subjective sleep quality
findings.quote: The results show a positive correlation between vertical illuminance and sleep quality.

findings.antecedent: lighting levels of at least 1000 lux on the eye
findings.consequent: biological stimulation
findings.quote: Many studies... indicate that lighting levels of at least 1000 lux on the eye are needed for biological stimulation.

findings.antecedent: cooler light colours (5000-6000 K) for biological stimulation
findings.consequent: lower required lighting level (e.g., 60% of 3000 K light for same melatonin suppression)
findings.quote: By using somewhat cooler light colours (5000-6000 K) at the moments when biological stimulation is wanted, this required lighting level could be somewhat lower than 1000 lux

findings.antecedent: dynamic artificial lighting (changing colour and lighting level)
findings.consequent: creation of conditions for action and relaxation
findings.quote: The changing colour and lighting level of dynamic artificial lighting can help to create the conditions needed for this

findings.antecedent: dynamic lighting scenario (stimulating cool-white high-level light in morning, gradually warmer/lower level, minimum 500 lux at lunchtime (warm-white), sharp rise after lunch, gradual decrease, short 'booster' of cool-white light before end of day)
findings.consequent: positive effect on well-being and productivity
findings.quote: Such a "human" rhythm is expected to have a positive effect on well-being, and this in turn should have extra positive effects on productivity.

findings.antecedent: timing and duration of lighting
findings.consequent: biological effects
findings.quote: Biologically, however, the timing of the periods of light (or darkness) and their duration plays an essential role

findings.antecedent: good lighting (considering visual and non-visual biological effects)
findings.consequent: better work performance (speed), fewer errors and rejects, better safety, fewer accidents, lower absenteeism
findings.quote: good lighting also leads to better work performance (speed), fewer errors and rejects, better safety, fewer accidents, and lower absenteeism.

findings.antecedent: increased lighting level from 300 to 500 lux (for moderately difficult visual task)
findings.consequent: productivity increase
findings.quote: From 300 to 500 lux -> 8% Productivity increase

findings.antecedent: increased lighting level from 300 to 2000 lux (for moderately difficult visual task)
findings.consequent: productivity increase
findings.quote: From 300 to 2000 lux -> 20% Productivity increase

findings.antecedent: working indoors (40-200 times less light than outdoors)
findings.consequent: negative influence on health and well-being
findings.quote: The consequence of this was 40-200 times less light for those not working very close to a window. We have now learned that this has a negative influence on health and well-being.

findings.antecedent: sufficient biologically active light at needed moments (dynamic in level and colour, including cool white light)
findings.consequent: healthy people remain healthy, energy savings
findings.quote: We do this by ensuring that they receive sufficient biologically active light at the moments when this is needed. Lighting-daylight as well as artificial light-that is dynamic in both level and colour is the key in this respect. Using cool white light at moments that biologically active lighting is required is important; because it lowers the lighting level required and thus enables saving on energy costs.

limitations: The detailed effects of light on circadian rhythms in rapidly rotating shifts still require further investigations before final general recommendations can be made (De Groot, 2005).
The detailed effects of light on nighttime lighting for shift workers still require further investigations before final general recommendations can be made (De Groot, 2005).
minimum_safe_summary: This narrative review synthesizes research on the non-visual biological effects of lighting, highlighting that light entering the human eye, beyond vision, significantly impacts health, well-being, alertness, and sleep quality. Key findings indicate that a novel photoreceptor (ipRGC) in the eye regulates circadian rhythms and hormone production, with maximum biological sensitivity in the blue light spectrum. Good lighting, particularly bright morning light and dynamic lighting scenarios that adjust level and color temperature throughout the day, can synchronize the body's internal clock, reduce stress, improve alertness, and enhance sleep quality. The paper also presents evidence that improved lighting levels lead to increased productivity. Limitations include the need for further detailed investigations into light's effects on rapidly rotating shift workers and nighttime lighting.
